changes.text: This chapter identifies the transactions that VisaNet supports for full service point of service (POS), gives a brief description of each transaction type, and explains how full service participants maintain message integrity for transactions. The term mandatory refers to a client requirement and means a field must be present in a message and must contain certain values. Conditional refers to a client requirement applying under specified conditions. While the V.I.P. System enforces edits and rejects transactions for some violations of mandatory requirements, V.I.P. does not enforce edits for all mandatory or conditional fields and values. Visa strongly urges clients and their processors to comply with mandatory field requirements. Failure to do so can result in greater risk to the client or increased processing cost, and may result in exposure to disputes and compliance claims, elevated decline rates, and disqualification for preferential interchange rates. Visa also advises clients not to rely on the V.I.P. System to reject all transactions not complying with mandatory or conditional requirements.

text_a: There are three types of interchange reimbursement fees (IRFs).

Domestic Interchange Reimbursement Fees—Fees paid by one participant to another for transactions acquired and issued in the same country. Intraregional Interchange Reimbursement Fees—Fees paid by one participant to another for transactions acquired and issued in different countries within the same Visa region. Interregional Interchange Reimbursement Fees—Fees paid by one participant to another for transactions acquired and issued in different Visa regions. In this context, transaction country is the country in which the transaction takes place, and issuing country is the country of the issuer of the card used in the transaction. If no domestic IRF has been established, the intraregional IRF applies. If no intraregional IRF has been established, the interregional (international) IRF applies. IRFs are settled daily through the settlement process. For National Net Settlement Service transactions, there is only one settlement currency, so balancing does not involve currency conversion. For International Settlement Service transactions, however, there are many settlement currencies. Visa uses buy and sell rates for currency conversion. These rates are paired into USD-based rates used when converting non- USD currencies against the U.S. dollar, and cross-rates (non-USD-based rates) used for selected currencies in which the rates quoted are against a currency other than the U.S. dollar. The Multicurrency Service automatically converts the transaction currency to the acquirer's settlement currency (if the two are different), and automatically converts the cardholder's billing currency to the issuer's settlement currency (if the two are different), to one of the settlement currencies. For POS transactions, IRFs are typically paid by acquirers to issuers. Fees for manual cash disbursements, reversals, merchandise returns, dispute financials, and credit adjustments flow in the opposite direction. text_a: Purchase With Cashback – Cashback is a variation of the purchase transaction permitting the cardholder to get cash in addition to goods or services. Cashback is a domestic service available to participating Visa regions for their issuers, acquirers, and merchants. The VisaNet Cashback Service identifies the cashback amount separately in authorization messages and in settlement to allow issuers to make authorization decisions and to monitor cash activity for their cardholders, Clients can contact their Visa representatives for additional information on cashback features, controls, and availability. Quasi-Cash – Quasi-cash is a variation of the purchase transaction, used for the purchase of items directly convertible to cash, such as gaming chips and money orders. It is available for Visa POS and Interlink. VisaNet does not support American Express Quasi-cash transactions. Key-Entered Purchase – This transaction is a variation of the purchase transaction, used only for Visa POS transactions when the magnetic stripe on the card is not readable. Purchase With Address Verification – This transaction is used by such merchants as direct marketing firms and airlines to verify a cardholder's address as part of a purchase request. This transaction is available for Visa POS.

Account Funding Transaction – This transaction is used to fund accounts such as brokerage accounts and online stored value cards, from a Visa debit or credit card. Original Credit Transaction – This transaction enables funds to be credited to Visa account numbers for a purpose other than refunding a Visa purchase. Deferred Clearing Purchase Transaction – This transaction is used by such merchants as hotels and car rental agencies when the full purchase amount is not known at the time of transaction authorization. This transaction, used only by Visa POS acquirers, involves an authorization request followed by a deferred clearing advice message. Merchandise Return – A merchandise return transaction enables merchants to credit the account of a Visa POS cardholder who returns merchandise. Balance Inquiry – Balance inquiry transactions enable cardholders to check their balances at stand-alone merchant terminals and at the point of sale. If the issuer system cannot be reached, V.I.P. stand-in processing responds that issuer is not available. If the issuer is available and supports balance inquiries, VisaNet returns the account balance to the acquirer for display or for printing in the currency of the merchant or of the ATM. Issuers can optionally provide balance information in Visa POS purchase transaction responses. However, for an 0200 POS eFunds transactions (network 0029), the acquirer receives balance information in Field 54 – Additional Amounts regardless of the issuer's selected response options. (This processing does not apply to stand-alone balance inquiries.) ATM acquirers in the U.S. region must support balance inquiries; support of this transaction is optional for all other participants. PINs are required for full service 0200 POS balance inquiries. PINs may not be required if a chip card is being used in a full service 0100 POS balance inquiries. Address Verification Only (Visa POS) – This transaction is used by merchants like direct marketing firms and airlines to verify a cardholder's address before submitting a purchase transaction. Incremental Authorizations – Merchants use incremental authorization transactions when final purchase amounts are unknown. Incremental authorizations enable merchants to obtain approval on additional amount, after the merchant uses an estimated amount to initiate and authorize the original transaction. Merchants can only do an incremental authorization in conjunction with an estimated authorization. When merchants determine final amounts, they submit supplemental, incremental authorization, or authorization reversal for cancelled purchases. Endpoints must not decline incremental authorizations by treating them as duplicate. In incremental authorization requests and their reversals, field 11 and field 37 values matches corresponding values in original authorization requests and the Transaction identifier (TID) value matches corresponding values in original authorization responses. Acquirers perform clearing using a single clearing transaction for the final amount, the issuer can match the incremental authorizations to the original estimated amount. Participating CPS POS Acquirers must include the TID from the initial authorization in any subsequent incremental authorization request or reversal.

Field 62.2 – Transaction Identifier must be present in back-office exception transactions; otherwise, the exceptions are rejected with reason code 0153 or 0483. Visa issuers and acquirers must support exception-related transactions. Issuer systems must be able to create dispute financials and to receive adjustments and dispute response financials. Acquirer systems must be able to receive dispute financials and to create adjustments and dispute response financials. Because authorization is not required and exception-related transactions cannot be declined, V.I.P. always processes them as advices. In addition, Visa POS issuers must be able to create dispute financial reversals, and participating acquirers must be able to receive them. Each type of exception transaction is described in this section. Adjustment (Back-Office)—An acquirer initiates an adjustment to an original transaction to correct an error, such as an out-of-balance condition at the POS. The adjustment can be a debit or a credit (because the cardholder's account was charged less or more than the actual amount agreed on at the time of the transaction). VisaNet supports adjustment transactions for Visa transactions. Dispute Financial—A dispute financial transaction is used to credit a cardholder's (or customer's) account for the purchase amount under certain conditions. An issuer can initiate a dispute financial when: A cardholder disputes a transaction. A cardholder asserts merchandise was returned but a merchandise credit transaction has not been received by the issuer. The issuer itself disputes a transaction. The issuer receives an unpostable debit adjustment from an acquirer.

VisaNet supports dispute financial transactions for Visa transactions. Dispute Financial Reversal—Visa issuers can initiate a dispute financial reversal to cancel a prior dispute financial transaction sent in error to the acquirer. Dispute Response Financial—Acquirers can initiate a dispute response financial transaction to debit a cardholder's account when the validity of a dispute financial can be disproved. The dispute response financial must be for the exact amount of the dispute financial. Dispute financials, dispute financial reversals, and dispute response financials must contain field 136 and field 137 if the original message contains them.

section_new_paragraphs: Visa Stop Payment Service (VSPS) allows issuers, on behalf of their cardholders, to stop unwanted future payments from debiting an account. Examples of payments that may be stopped include subscriptions or membership fees that a merchant continues to charge despite a cardholder’s attempts to cancel. Participating issuers place stop instructions in the portfolio file (PF) in the V.I.P. cardholder database (CDB). If acquirers submit a VSPS eligible transaction, V.I.P. checks the database, and if it encounters a stop instruction for that account number, it declines the request. There are three implementation options for Visa Stop Payment Service (VSPS) that can be combined to suit clients' needs:

The Visa-recommended implementation option for a fast implementation is the VSPS user interface. Access to optional reporting is available for all implementation options through the VSPS user interface.

VSPS Stop Instruction ID: The VSPS stop instruction ID is the unique reference for each stop instruction. The value is generated by V.I.P. and must be provided for inquiry, replace, and delete. VSPS Stop Restrictions: Stop restrictions can be optionally included in merchant level stop instructions to limit the range of transactions to be stopped. These stop restrictions are available:

Field 4 — Amount, Transaction: If the amount is present in the stop instruction, eligible transactions can only be stopped for that amount. If amount is not present, eligible transactions can be stopped for any amount. Field 18 — Merchant Category Code: If an MCC is present in the stop instruction, eligible transactions can only be stopped if they contain that MCC. If MCC is not present in the stop instruction, eligible transaction can be stopped for any MCC. TLV Field 127.PF, Dataset ID 69, Tag DF15 and DF 16 — Minimum Amount and Maximum Amount: If either or both restrictions are present in the stop instruction, eligible transaction can only be stopped for transaction amount within the specified amount range. TLV Field 127.PF, Dataset ID 69, Tag DF18 — Recurring/ Installment Indicator: If this tag contains a 1 (Restrict), eligible transactions can only be stopped if the acquirer identifies the transactions as recurring or installments in field 126.13 or field 60.8. changes.old: The Dynamic Key Exchange (DKE) Service is an optional service that enables clients to change Data Encryption Standard (DES) cryptographic keys with VisaNet through the use of online 0800 and 0810 messages. For a comprehensive description of the DKE Service, refer to V.I.P. System Overview and Services. The following fields in the 0800 request are used for a DKE Service key exchange request: Field 11—System Trace Audit Number Field 33—Forwarding Institution Identification Code Field 39—Response Code Field 48, Usage 14—Dynamic Key Exchange Working Key Check Value Field 52—Personal Identification Number (PIN) Data Field 53—Security-Related Control Information Field 63.1—Network ID Code Field 70—Network Management Information Code Field 105—Double-Length DES Key (Triple DES) Field 110—Encryption Data (TLV Format) Clients use 0800 requests to request and to deliver new working keys for PIN encryption; clients use 0810 responses to acknowledge their receipt. The 0800 message initiator, which can be a participating acquirer or issuer, or V.I.P., assigns the trace number (in field 11). Clients must return the trace number unchanged in the 0810 response. If a request must be re-sent, its trace number comes from the original request. The message originator must indicate which key is to be changed in Field 53—Security-Related Control Information. Acquirers can begin using the new key after the 0810 response is sent to V.I.P. For acquirers supporting a single working key, V.I.P. has the option of processing messages with the new key or with the old key for five minutes. After five minutes, all acquirer-initiated messages must have PINs encrypted with the new working key. For issuers, V.I.P. begins using the new key upon receipt of the 0810 response (in which the code in Field 39—Response Code is 00). For issuers supporting a single working key, they immediately update their copy of the key upon receipt of the 0800 request from V.I.P. V.I.P. continues sending messages with the old key until it receives the 0810 response. Therefore, single-key issuers must keep a copy of the old key until V.I.P. begins using the new one. If V.I.P. encounters PIN block errors during standard message processing, V.I.P. returns response code 81 (cryptographic error found) in PIN in the 0800 request and initiates an automatic acquirer key change. If the issuer encounters a PIN block error during verification, it returns response code 81 in the 0810 response. V.I.P. initiates an automatic issuer working key change.

STIP checks cardholder activity using these:
Issuer-specified activity limits (count and amount). Alternative limits designated on the Account Screen Authorization File (ASAF).

The activity check determines whether or not approval of the request causes the card usage to exceed these limits. If the activity is over the specified limits, STIP assigns response code 61 (exceeds approval amount limit). The activity check is based on activity accumulated daily in the Activity File by default, which contains only STIP approvals. Issuers may optionally specify that both issuer and STIP approvals are accumulated in the activity file. VisaNet resets the accumulated totals in the Activity File to zero every 24 hours so that the file always reflects the current day's activity. Activity Checking and Accumulation When a transaction is processed in STIP, V.I.P. performs activity checking and accumulation using the issuer-specified activity limits. Accumulators are running totals of transactions approved in STIP. While issuers specify activity limits at the issuing identifier level, V.I.P. maintains accumulators at the account level. This description of activity checking and accumulation assumes that the combination of issuer specifications and transaction characteristics would result in activity checking being performed, and, that the transaction passed all other STIP tests. A transaction passes activity checking if adding the current transaction to the accumulators would not cause the accumulators to exceed the limits. Failing a limit (activity count, activity, amount, or maximum transaction size) prevents STIP approval. Accumulators are incremented only when the transaction passes all STIP tests, and STIP sends an approval to the acquirer. Transactions approved by the issuer, do not increment accumulators unless the issuer has specified this option. For example: 1.

If the sum of the daily STIP activity count, and preauthorization count plus one (for this transaction) is greater than the STIP limit for the applicable Purchase (POS) or cash category, STIP sets the activity check response to response code 65 (exceeds withdrawal frequency limit). 2. If the sum is not greater than the applicable purchase (POS) or cash activity limit STIP processing continues.

section_new_paragraphs: The Cardholder Authentication Verification Value (CAVV) Verification Service provides the functionality to verify that the CAVV submitted by an acquirer in a Visa Secure (formerly known as Verified by Visa (VbV)) authorization message matches the CAVV generated by VisaNet or by an issuer's Access Control Server (ACS) during authentication. The CAVV is a cryptographic value generated by the issuer and sent to the merchant during the authentication process in a Visa Secure transaction. The verification process involves two phases: 1.

During the Visa Secure phase, the issuer or V.I.P. electronically identifies the cardholder and generates a CAVV that is associated with the purchase or financial transaction. The CAVV Verification Service begins when the acquirer submits the authorization or the full financial message and includes the CAVV that was generated during the Visa Secure phase in the request. When the CAVV is present in the transaction, the issuer or V.I.P. verifies that the CAVV in the message matches the CAVV generated during the Visa Secure phase. If the CAVV is verified, the transaction is protected from certain chargebacks should disputes arise later. When the validation is completed, the issuer or V.I.P. populates the results in the CAVV Results Code field depending on which entity performed the validation. The value in this field indicates the outcome of the validation, which entity performed the validation, and the classification of the transaction (Authentication, Attempt, or non-secure). Reject Code 0193 in the CAVV results code field indicates that the CAVV is invalid. To validate the CAVV, the issuer or V.I.P. uses Data Encryption Standard (DES) keys and other CAVV parameters to calculate the CAVV and compare it to the CAVV generated by the ACS. Issuers that choose to have Visa perform verification on their behalf must provide Visa with their DES keys.

Visa offers two CAVV Verification Service processing options to issuers that participate in Visa Secure: Authentication or Attempt. Authentication—With this option, the issuer is a full participant in the service and has cardholders enrolled in Visa Secure. Transactions are classified as Authentication transactions when the acquirer, the issuer, and the cardholder all participate in Visa Secure. Attempt—With this option, the issuer or V.I.P. generates a CAVV for attempted transactions. Transactions submitted by a participating acquirer are classified as Attempts when the issuer or cardholder does not participate in Visa Secure. Liability shifts for these types of transactions. This option is mandatory in some regions. Visa encourages issuers to participate in both. Both allow issuers to select a predefined process by which their transactions are to be processed in Normal mode and in Stand-In Processing (STIP) mode: Standard Issuer CAVV Service/Standard Decline/Failure Option—With this option, V.I.P. performs all validations on the issuer's behalf, declines transactions when the CAVV validation fails, and forwards the status results of transactions that were not declined to the issuer. All CAVV Verification Results to the Issuer Option—With this option, V.I.P. performs all validations on the issuer's behalf and forwards all status results of transactions to the issuer. Issuer Supports Own CAVV Verification Option—With this option, VisaNet forwards the transactions to the issuer to perform validation. The issuer returns the status results in the response messages. If issuers participating in the CAVV Verification Service have VisaNet perform CAVV validation, V.I.P. performs the verification before acting upon issuer availability. The Visa Security Module (VSM) uses authentication data elements in Field 126.9—CAVV Data and Field 126.8— Transaction ID (XID) (or just field 126.9 if Field 126.9, usage 3—3-D Secure CAVV, Revised Format is being used) along with issuer-supplied keys. A card verification value (CVV) is a 3-digit number encoded on the card's physical magnetic stripe or in the chip's image on a Visa Smart Debit/Smart Credit (VSDC) card. An Integrated Chip Card card verification value (iCVV) is a 3-digit number issuers may encode in the chip's image on a VSDC chip card instead of the CVV. (The iCVV is also referred to as the alternate CVV.) A VSDC card's chip image may contain the CVV or iCVV. A card's physical magnetic stripe does not use an iCVV. The Card Verification Value 2 (CVV2) is an embossed 3-digit security number appearing on the reverse side of the card. A customized option is also allowed for placement of the CVV2 on standard Visa cards. The CVV2 may be printed directly on the card background, on either the front or back of the card. Clients can use the CVV2 in card-present and card-not-present transactions.
Card Verification Value (CVV or iCVV) for card-present transactions. Card Verification Value 2 (CVV2) for card-present and card-not-present transactions.

The CPS/Account Funding program requirements include the CVV2 for electronic commerce (e- commerce) stored-value transactions. For stored-value cards refilled more than once, the program requires the CVV2 only in the initial funding request for the request to qualify; subsequent transactions can qualify for the CPS program without the CVV2 being present. CVV and iCVV—Determining whether the CVV or the iCVV requires verification depends on the issuer's system parameters and on the code in Field 22—Point-of-Service Entry Mode Code in the request. Also, the verification entity performs CVV processing only if the CVV is in the
correct position in the track. Refer to the Payment Technology Standards Manual for technical specifications for CVV placement.

If field 22, positions 1 and 2, contain 90 or 05 and the issuer's system settings indicate V.I.P. is to perform CVV checking, the security module performs the verification using the CVV algorithm. Validation of the CVV from the physical magnetic stripe does not occur if field 22, positions 1 and 2, contain 02 or 95, because the values 02 and 95 indicate the track data in Field 35—Track 2 Data or in Field 45—Track 1 Data may be unreliable and accurate CVV processing may not be possible. For Plus ATM transactions only, the value 02 indicates the exact contents of Track 2 were read and CVV checking is possible. For Visa ATM and Interlink transactions, acquirers can use values 02 or 90 to indicate the complete, unaltered magnetic stripe content has been read and CVV processing may not be possible. If field 22, positions 1 and 2, contain 05, V.I.P. assumes the track data originated from the chip. V.I.P. checks the issuer's system settings (in CORE) to determine if the verification value in the track data is a CVV or an iCVV. (Set A indicates a CVV; Set B indicates an iCVV.)

If the issuer's system settings indicate it supports CVV checking for chip cards but does not support iCVV checking, the security module performs the verification using the CVV algorithm. If the issuer's system parameters indicate it supports CVV checking and iCVV checking for chip cards, the security module performs the verification using the CVV algorithm except the system substitutes 999 for the service restriction code. The presence of code 90 in field 22 does not guarantee CVV processing. If a non- participating acquirer submits code 90 in field 22, V.I.P. rejects the message.

Validation of the CVV or the iCVV residing in the chip's magnetic stripe image does not occur if field 22, positions 1 and 2, contain 95, because the value 95 indicates the track data in field 35 or in field 45 may be unreliable.

To verify the CVV, V.I.P. (or the issuer) uses the DES key and other information from the stripe to calculate a CVV and compares it with the stripe's encoded CVV. For the CVV to be valid, the two values must match exactly; otherwise, the CVV fails validation. As indicated above, iCVV processing uses all options, parameters, and keys used in CVV processing. V.I.P. or the issuer uses the same algorithm for the CVV and for the iCVV, but they substitute the value 999 for the service restriction code for iCVV processing. As part of the issuer participation procedure, the issuer specifies expiration date ranges and whether the CVV check is to be based on the chip image of the magnetic stripe data. STIP can respond to CVV failures with an issuer-specified decline response code or can forward failures to the issuer for processing. Issuers or V.I.P. can approve, refer, or decline transactions failing CVV validation depending on issuer-specified parameters. Refer to the Card Verification Value (CVV) Service chapter in V.I.P. System Overview and Services, for a description of the service. Refer to the Payment Technology Standards Manual for technical specifications for CVV placement, calculation, and verification.
